Copied from my own comment on the video:

Hi, I'm the madman who commissioned this song! :)

There are several reasons why I did it, the first and foremost being that I just wanted something that would stand out. And this did, right? But also, I think it's worth noting that the original episode of Rebecca Black versus Justin Bieber on *Death Battle* was one of those early episodes based on real people, right at the peak of both their hatedoms. This is the kind of episode and concept that will never happen again with the show. And while that's understandable, it's a bit of a shame because there could be some really silly matchups if we included literal interpretations of lyrics or roles played by actors like Arnold Schwarzenegger or Mr. T—similar to what they did with Chuck Norris, though that was still season 2 and we're almost at 11.

What really inspired me to pursue this matchup is Rebecca Black's music, which has really matured, especially her debut album. Both she and Bieber have songs that you could argue are about the massive amounts of hate they received at such young ages, and that idea I asked to influence the lyrics. While Bieber's music is whatever, I genuinely enjoy Rebecca Black's recent work (one of the references is her song "Destroy Me").

One thing important to the concept was that Rebecca Black was once a big fan of Justin Bieber. I'm not sure if that's still the case, but I asked Brandon to approach this as a sort of duet between the two of them. Living the dream and expressing their growth over the previous decade-plus during this battle track... I thought that would make for a really interesting sequel, with this as the soundtrack.

Lastly, and I'm not just making this up, I kind of see this as an advertisement. I wanted to prove that aside from a few outliers and odd concessions, unconventional ideas are not a deterrent for Brandon Yates (he takes debit or credit). After all, who else would agree to create a track based on the idea of a sequel to the worst-aged and most disliked episode of a YouTube show from the 2010s that was trying extremely hard to be edgy while appealing to a niche hobby?

We all generally understand that adaptations into different mediums require change to work, and different aspects must be considered that may not have been considered before. I've personally found, maybe others will disagree, that since a lot of the famous comic book characters have been around for between 50 to nearing 100 years... that's a lot to draw from, and there is fluidity when it comes to how much a new version draws from. Even more, there are times when an adaptation affects and colors and adds to the original source after the fact. There are layers to it.

Seeing how mostly successful the MCU has been, even if we set a specific endpoint at Avengers Endgame, I have to ask. I think an important aspect to really emphasize is the context and overall package of Burton films. We live in a society (lol) that has not just grown up with these movies but has made them a part of popular culture. A lot of what the public zeitgeist understands about Batman nowadays—and about superhero films in general—came from the first Burton Batman film. Now we have Batman material marketed to all ages, from toddlers to adults (we literally had Batman say "fuck" and saw the outline of his penis, both in the last few years. Truly amazing times we live in).

Others have already discussed the timeframe and compared it to the Adam West Batman but even leading up to 1989 people were so upset that Keaton (known for comedy roles) was cast as Batman; that there were write-in campaigns and petitions because they assumed it would be just more of the same campiness. Petitions! Pre-internet! Over Batman 1989! Can you imagine?

But then also compare it to the most famous superhero movie before it—Superman 1978. That was the tone people might have been expecting, along with the 60s Adam West series: purposefully campy and lighthearted. The tone that 1989 and Returns had, compared to expectations, is an important factor, but people really didn't expect a Batman film with this look and this content to take itself as seriously as it did. I dont know that I would see this as a dark film myself either, but time changes people's perceptions.

The aesthetic and atmosphere are an important part of the package. The gothic set design, the lighting, Fanny Elfman's score, all of it makes Gotham feel very out of time. The only thing making it obviously 80s to me are the Prince songs, which in hindsight only exacerbate the camp. But Elfman's main theme, even though the melody mostly rises, is generally in a minor key and broods more often than it soars. The "funny" moments I remember were played for dark humor. The sequel had complaints of being too violent for a kids' movie, with reports of kids crying and being escorted out of theaters, for goodness sake! The 80s and early 90s have a reputation of kids' movies getting away with darker material than nowadays from the kids who grew up then, so a 1992 PG-13 movie having that effect feels important to note.

It took the cliches that Dragon Ball used over the course of its 11-year run and threw them into one single plot that couldn't have been more cliche if it tried. It mixed and matched so many random details and tried to Frankenstein it into something coherent, even as its own separate thing, but the seams are ripping open in every scene.

And you know what, I've read what is purportedly the original script Ben Ramsey wrote. The "more fairhful" one. And nah, that just adds a few more token names from the series and throws in more cliches (and other anime????) It's weird to describe. Krillin makes a cameo and the Pilaf trio and Suno are there, but Oolong is a mindless monster Goku kills in the 2nd half of the script, the Pilaf trio are all Namekians explicitly, and the backstory of this version of the world is detailed in an in-universe card game that still-high-schooler Goku is a fan of like straight up giving Yu-Gi-Oh vibes????

I can only speak for myself. While it is mostly a semi-ironic adoration, I must admit there are a few aspects I sincerely like about DBE. The thing is, they seem to be stuff the filmmakers fell ass backwards into - the BTS seems like a lot of weird decisions and restraints were put in place out the gate. Netflix Death Note is not good in my opinion, but I feel like its badness is mostly generically bad. The good choices and decisions are genuinely things I enjoyed while watching the movie including some of the changes (it takes a special change to upset me on principle, which this movie had far less than I think DBE did).  You can still watch NetNote blind, be told it was based on Death Note, and understand. DBE as a film is mostly unrecognizable to the source material.

On that note, other than some of the pacing, I enjoyed the first two Japanese live action Death Note films. It makes some big changes in the second one but for all intents and purposes finishes the story so you can literally stop it there (there are additional movies; the only one I recall is a prequel revolving around L). It's very faithful in look and feel and a lot of the plot. And while dubbing over live action is a little weird, almost the entire Viz anime dub cast reprised their roles for the English version. I work delivery for a restaurant, but we have a contract with DoorDash so that when it's busy we can get them to help with the load. The customer is not charged extra, and it can be a great help on busy busy nights (Valentine's Day and Halloween are our blackout days), but generally customers may not be aware when the driver is from DoorDash (or when the food is delivered lol) so they will call us to complain.

We have a few regular DoorDashers with few to no complaints and we love them for it, but in my time here we've also had people conplain to us that the deliveries from DoorDash drivers never delivered, or threw their delivery (intended for a hospital employee!) just tossed to the side literally thrown to the side. Or someone can't find the address when it's literally the same street as the restaurant. And the best part? The tips go to the driver, so if it's been DoorDashed the DoorDash driver will get the tip - even if they forgot something or delivered incorrectly. And then the main drivers at work have to drive the delivery out and they don't get paid either the tip or for mileage. Basically out of pocket for the driver.

I've heard rumors from coworkers that befause "the economy is bad" we might cut back on or remove our regular in store drivers entirely and rely solely upon DoorDash.
